items.followUp: Why does BF₃ act as a Lewis acid?

rubric.why: Shows that boron does not have a complete octet.
rubric.description: Boron has only six electrons in its outer shell in BF₃.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that boron has six outer-shell electrons or an incomplete octet.

rubric.why: Explains the consequence of boron's electron deficiency.
rubric.description: BF₃ can accept a lone pair of electrons.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that BF₃ accepts a lone pair of electrons.

modelAnswer: In BF₃, boron has only six electrons in its outer shell, so it has an incomplete octet.
Therefore, BF₃ is electron deficient and can accept a lone pair of electrons.

items.followUp: Define intramolecular forces and give one example.

rubric.why: Identifies the nature of the forces and that they act between molecules.
rubric.description: Intermolecular forces are attractive forces between molecules.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a definition that states the forces are attractions between molecules.

rubric.why: Provides a valid example of an attraction between molecules.
rubric.description: A hydrogen bond between water molecules is an example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for one valid example.

modelAnswer: Intermolecular forces are attractive forces that act between molecules.
A hydrogen bond between water molecules is an example.

items.followUp: Why is air considered a mixture?

rubric.why: Shows that the components of a solution are combined physically rather than chemically.
rubric.description: The substances in a solution are physically mixed, not chemically combined.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the components are physically mixed or not chemically combined.

rubric.why: Gives a characteristic of mixtures that applies to solutions.
rubric.description: The components retain their properties and can be present in variable proportions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that components retain their properties, have variable proportions, or can be separated by physical methods.

modelAnswer: The solute and solvent are physically mixed and are not chemically combined.
Their proportions can vary, and the components retain their properties; therefore, a solution is a mixture.

items.followUp: Why is carbonic acid considered a weak electrolyte?

rubric.why: States that only a small fraction of the acid molecules form ions in solution.
rubric.description: CH₃COOH ionizes only partially in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that it ionizes or dissociates partially in water.

rubric.why: Connects partial ionization to its weak electrolytic behaviour.
rubric.description: The small number of ions formed makes it a weak conductor of electricity.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for linking the few ions or reversible ionization to weak electrical conductivity.

modelAnswer: CH₃COOH ionizes only partially in water, producing relatively few ions.
Because it has few ions to carry charge, it conducts electricity weakly and is a weak electrolyte.

items.followUp: How does ionization energy affect the electropositivity of an element?

rubric.why: States the direction of the relationship between the two properties.
rubric.description: Electropositivity and ionization energy are inversely related.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the relationship is inverse or opposite.

rubric.why: Explains the relationship in terms of how readily an atom loses electrons.
rubric.description: An element with low ionization energy loses electrons readily and is more electropositive.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly relating low ionization energy to high electropositivity, or high ionization energy to low electropositivity.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity is inversely related to ionization energy.
An element with low ionization energy loses electrons more readily and is more electropositive.

items.followUp: Write any four physical properties of copper.

rubric.why: Recognizes two valid properties of platinum.
rubric.description: Any two valid properties of platinum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each pair of distinct valid properties, up to 2 marks total.

rubric.why: Recognizes two additional valid properties of platinum.
rubric.description: Any two further valid properties of platinum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for each additional pair of distinct valid properties, up to 2 marks total; award no more than 2 marks for this question.

modelAnswer: Platinum is lustrous.
It is malleable and ductile.
It has a high melting point.
It resists corrosion.

rubric.why: Locates transition metals in the periodic table.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying them as d-block elements.

rubric.description: Their atoms or common ions have partially filled d orbitals.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that the d orbitals or subshell are partially filled in their atoms or common ions.

modelAnswer: Transition metals are d-block elements whose atoms or common ions have partially filled d orbitals.

items.followUp: Describe the observations and conclusions of the gold-foil experiment.

rubric.why: States the main observation for the majority of alpha particles.
rubric.description: Most alpha particles passed straight through the foil without deflection.

rubric.why: States the observation for a smaller number of alpha particles.
rubric.description: A few alpha particles were deflected from their paths.

rubric.why: States the rare observation of particles turning back or being strongly deflected.
rubric.description: Very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or bounced back.

rubric.why: Gives the conclusion drawn from the strong deflections and rebounds.
rubric.description: The atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of its mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the small, dense, positively charged nucleus.

rubric.why: Gives the conclusion drawn from most alpha particles passing through undeflected.
rubric.description: Most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that most of the atom is empty space.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without any deflection.
A few alpha particles were deflected from their original paths.
Very few alpha particles were deflected through large angles or bounced back.
These results showed that the atom has a small, dense, positively charged nucleus containing most of its mass.
Most of the atom is empty space.
